extracted.intended_audience: scientists, bibliometricians, science policy analysts, and research librarians
extracted.subtask_description: Analyzing the statistical properties and structure of scientific citation networks (distribution of citations, age effects, research fronts, and bibliographic service needs). Includes empirical metrics (e.g., immediacy factor, half-life) and network/topographic descriptions used to evaluate and map scientific literatures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distribution of citations per paper (empirical percentages)
rubrics_metrics.description: In any given year about 35 percent of all the existing papers are not cited at all, and another 49 percent are cited only once; leaving about 16 percent cited more than once (breakdown: ~9% twice, ~3% three times, ~2% four times, ~1% five times, ~1% six times or more).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these empirical proportions (from Garfield's 1961 data) as a baseline for assessing how frequently papers are cited in a single year; the data imply a long tail of more-heavily-cited papers and a large fraction with zero or one citation per year.

rubrics_metrics.name: Average citation rate (long-run)
rubrics_metrics.description: Over the long run and over the entire world literature, we should find that, on the average, every scientific paper ever is cited about once a year (an average of about 1 citation per paper per year).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat ~1 citation/paper/year as a standard expected baseline when modeling long-term citation flows; deviations for age-specific cohorts (recent vs old papers) should be interpreted relative to this standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power-law (heavy-tail) decline of highly-cited papers
rubrics_metrics.description: The number of papers receiving many citations appears to decrease roughly as a power law (the paper suggests decreases of order n^{-2.5} or n^{-3}).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect a rapid decline in counts of papers as citation count increases; model the tail of the citation-count distribution with heavy-tail / power-law fits rather than normal distributions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Probability of being cited at least once per year ('live' papers)
rubrics_metrics.description: For 'live' papers the chance of being cited at least once in any year is about 60 percent; about 10 percent of all papers 'die' every year and are not cited again.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When projecting lifetime impact, incorporate a per-year survival/citation probability (~60% for live papers) and a non-negligible annual attrition (~10%).

rubrics_metrics.name: Immediacy factor (age-dependent concentration on recent work)
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'immediacy factor' quantifies the 'bunching' of citations to recent papers: roughly 30 percent of citations account for the immediacy 'hump' (selective references to recent literature) while about 70 percent follow the longer-term growth curve.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the immediacy factor to separate random/background citation behavior (70%) from selective recent-literature focus (30%); half of the 30% immediacy citations are to papers 1–6 years old. This helps identify the active research front.

rubrics_metrics.name: Age-decay / citation half-life (exponential decrease)
rubrics_metrics.description: The chance that a paper will be cited by a later paper decreases exponentially with age, roughly halving every ~13.5 years; for very recent papers (<15 years) citation rates are considerably higher than the standard value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model citation probability as an exponential decay with characteristic timescale ~13.5 years for older papers, but allow elevated rates (peaking around ~2.5 years) for recent papers that form the immediacy hump.

rubrics_metrics.name: Age-profile peak for recent papers
rubrics_metrics.description: Citation rate for papers rises for recent cohorts, reaching a maximum of about 6 times the standard value for papers ~2.5 years old, then declines for very recent papers that have not yet been noticed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating short-term impact, account for a pronounced peak in citation propensity a few years after publication (around 2–3 years), not just monotonic decay from publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiplicity (ratio of citations per cited paper) varies with age
rubrics_metrics.description: The multiplicity (number of citations per cited paper) falls off sharply with age; recent papers, when cited, contribute a larger fraction of citations relative to their availability in the literature than older papers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use multiplicity as a diagnostic of how concentrated citation attention is on recent work; plotting multiplicity by publication year helps reveal the research front and immediacy effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research front (tight knitted subset of literature)
rubrics_metrics.description: Each year's new papers are 'knitted' to a small, select part of earlier literature forming a tight pattern of multiple relationships — the 'research front' — distinct from a broader, weakly connected background.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify research fronts as small, densely interlinked subgraphs (tight diagonal strips in citation matrices); these represent active topics and distinguish sciences from other scholarship. Use matrices and linkage patterns to delineate fronts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Matrix/topography indicators (diagonal strip, centralness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Citation matrices of chronologically arranged papers show a dense strip near the diagonal (the research front) and sparser background noise; measures of centralness (position within the topography by journal, author, country) indicate relative importance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Map literature via citation matrices to identify central/strategic positions. Use journal/author/country overlap and centralness metrics derived from linkage patterns to prioritize or rank subjects, journals, or authors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two bibliographic service needs: alerting/indexing and classification
rubrics_metrics.description: (i) An alerting/indexing service to keep scientists informed of peer work (an 'alerting' index); (ii) a classification/taxonomy system to systematize and reduce the scattering of knowledge so items can be found and treated as part of a cumulative record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design bibliographic systems with both timely alerting (to support research-front awareness) and robust classification schemes (to map the lasting taxonomy of knowledge). Both services address different user needs: current awareness vs. long-term organization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two types of literature / differing half-lives (classic vs ephemeral)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence supports that literature comprises two types with very different half-lives — 'classics' (long half-lives) and 'ephemeral' papers (short half-lives); relative proportions vary by field (e.g., mathematics, geology, botany more 'classic'; molecular biology, engineering more 'ephemeral').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating fields or papers, adjust expectations of longevity and citation trajectories according to field-specific mixes of classic vs ephemeral literature; avoid one-size-fits-all half-life assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cumulative advantage / burstiness of heavy citation
rubrics_metrics.description: Heavy citation tends to occur in bursts, and there is a conjectured statistical regularity that the more a paper is cited the more likely it is to be cited thereafter (suggesting cumulative advantage).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In models and assessments, incorporate mechanisms for path-dependence (preferential attachment) and burst-like behavior rather than assuming independent, identically-distributed citation events.
